pairs.source_text: hoc opere instituto et mea ad te promissione debito defendere aduersus eos, qui conditori eius deos suos praeferunt, fili carissime Marcelline, suscepi, magnum opus et arduum, sed Deus adiutor noster est.
pairs.question: Cui Augustinus opus De ciuitate Dei in praefatione dedicat atque inscribit?
pairs.question_en: To whom does Augustine dedicate and address the work City of God in the preface?
pairs.derivation: Preface fact: Augustine undertakes the work as owed by his promise and addresses it to 'fili carissime Marcelline.' Anchored to Augustine + the work; single-name answer (dative Marcellino), supported verbatim. Closed-book: the City of God's dedication to Marcellinus is standard. Source_text normalization: OCR doubling 'defeendere' corrected to 'defendere.'

pairs.source_text: An non etiam illi Romani Christi nomini infesti sunt, quibus propter Christum barbari pepercerunt? Testantur hoc martyrum loca et basilicae apostolorum, quae in illa uastatione Vrbis ad se confugientes suos alienosque receperunt.
pairs.question: In quae loca confugientes in illa uastatione Vrbis a barbarorum caede tuti fuerunt, ut Augustinus tradit?
pairs.answer: In basilicas apostolorum et martyrum loca.
pairs.question_en: Fleeing into which places were people kept safe from the barbarians' slaughter during that sack of the City, as Augustine relates?
pairs.answer_en: Into the basilicas of the apostles and the shrines of the martyrs.
pairs.derivation: The distinctive claim of Book 1: in the sack of Rome the barbarians spared those who took refuge in the Christian holy places. Anchored to Augustine + the sack of the City (uastatio Vrbis) + the barbari; the answer is the noun phrase supported verbatim ('martyrum loca et basilicae apostolorum'). Closed-book apologetic/historical fact, attributed with 'ut Augustinus tradit.' Note: Book 1 says only 'barbari' (not Goths/Alaric), so the agent is left general as in the text.

pairs.source_text: Lucretiam certe, matronam nobilem ueteremque Romanam, pudicitiae magnis efferunt laudibus. Huius corpore cum uiolenter oppresso Tarquinii regis filius libidinose potitus esset, illa scelus improbissimi iuuenis marito Collatino et propinquo Bruto, uiris clarissimis et fortissimis, indicauit eosque ad uindictam constrinxit.
pairs.question: A quo Lucretia, nobilis matrona Romana, uiolenter oppressa atque uitiata est?
pairs.question_en: By whom was Lucretia, the noble Roman matron, violently assaulted and ravished?
pairs.answer_en: By the son of King Tarquinius.
pairs.derivation: The famous Lucretia exemplum. Anchored to Lucretia (named, 'matrona nobilis ueteremque Romana'); single answer identifying the assailant by relation ('Tarquinii regis filius' = the son of King Tarquinius, i.e. Sextus Tarquinius), supported verbatim. Closed-book; the answer is kept to what the text states (the king's son) rather than the proper name Sextus. Source_text normalization: OCR 'uindicatam' corrected to 'uindictam.'

pairs.source_text: illa scelus improbissimi iuuenis marito Collatino et propinquo Bruto, uiris clarissimis et fortissimis, indicauit eosque ad uindictam constrinxit. Deinde foedi in se commissi aegra atque inpatiens se peremit.
pairs.question: Quid Lucretia fecit, postquam a Tarquinii regis filio uim perpessa scelus indicauit?
pairs.question_en: What did Lucretia do after, having suffered violence from the son of King Tarquinius, she had disclosed the crime?
pairs.derivation: The famous suicide of Lucretia. Anchored to Lucretia + the assault by Tarquin's son; short verifiable answer supported verbatim ('se peremit'; cf. 1.19 'male sibi consciam se peremit'). Closed-book: one of the most celebrated suicides in Roman legend. Source_text normalization: OCR 'e peremit' corrected to 'se peremit' and 'uindicatam' to 'uindictam.'

pairs.source_text: Marcus Regulus, imperator populi Romani, captiuus apud Carthaginienses fuit.
pairs.question: Apud quos captiuus fuit Marcus Regulus, imperator populi Romani?
pairs.question_en: Among whom was Marcus Regulus, a general of the Roman people, a captive?
pairs.derivation: Anchored to Marcus Regulus (named, 'imperator populi Romani'); single answer (the Carthaginians), supported verbatim. Closed-book: Regulus's captivity among the Carthaginians is a famous Roman exemplum.

pairs.source_text: ad hoc impetrandum etiam istum praecipue Regulum cum legatis suis Romam miserunt, prius iuratione constrictum, si quod uolebant minime peregisset, rediturum esse Carthaginem. Perrexit ille atque in senatu contraria persuasit, quoniam non arbitrabatur utile esse Romanae rei publicae mutare captiuos. Nec post hanc persuasionem a suis ad hostes redire compulsus est, sed quia iurauerat, id sponte compleuit.
pairs.question: Quo Marcus Regulus, iureiurando constrictus, ex urbe Roma ad hostes sponte rediit?
pairs.question_en: To where did Marcus Regulus, bound by his oath, voluntarily return from the city of Rome to the enemy?
pairs.derivation: The celebrated Regulus exemplum: bound by oath, he voluntarily returned to the Carthaginians rather than break faith. Anchored to Regulus + the oath; single place answer (Carthaginem), supported verbatim ('rediturum esse Carthaginem'; 'quia iurauerat, id sponte compleuit'). Closed-book.

pairs.source_text: Sed tamen etiam illi praeter Lucretiam, de qua supra satis quod uidebatur diximus, non facile reperiunt de cuius auctoritate praescribant, nisi illum Catonem, qui se Vticae occidit.
pairs.question: Quo in loco Cato se ipse occidit, ut Augustinus commemorat?
pairs.question_en: In what place did Cato kill himself, as Augustine recounts?
pairs.derivation: Anchored to Cato (the younger, Cato Uticensis) by his suicide; single place answer (locative Vticae), supported verbatim ('qui se Vticae occidit'). Closed-book: Cato's suicide at Utica is among the most famous in Roman history.

pairs.source_text: Cato enim numquam Caesarem uicerat, cui uictus dedignatus est subici et, ne subiceretur, a se ipso elegit occidi.
pairs.question: Cui uictori se subicere dedignatus Cato mortem sibi consciuit, ut Augustinus scribit?
pairs.question_en: To which victor did Cato disdain to submit, choosing instead to take his own life, as Augustine writes?
pairs.derivation: Anchored to Cato; single-name answer (dative Caesari), supported verbatim ('cui uictus dedignatus est subici et... a se ipso elegit occidi'). A distinct fact from the place of his death. Closed-book: Cato's refusal to live under Caesar's victory is famous.

pairs.source_text: Egregius Romani nominis Marcus Marcellus, qui Syracusas urbem ornatissimam cepit, refertur eam prius fleuisse ruituram et ante eius sanguinem suas illi lacrimas effudisse.
pairs.question: Quam urbem Marcus Marcellus cepit, ut Augustinus refert?
pairs.question_en: Which city did Marcus Marcellus capture, as Augustine relates?
pairs.derivation: Anchored to Marcus Marcellus; single place-name answer (Syracusas), supported verbatim ('qui Syracusas urbem ornatissimam cepit'). Closed-book: Marcellus's capture of Syracuse (212 BC) is a well-known historical fact. 'ut Augustinus refert' mirrors the text's 'refertur.'

pairs.source_text: Fabius, Tarentinae urbis euersor, a simulacrorum depraedatione se abstinuisse laudatur. Nam cum ei scriba suggessisset quid de signis deorum, quae multa capta fuerant, fieri iuberet, continentiam suam etiam iocando condiuit.
pairs.question: Cuius urbis euersor fuit ille Fabius qui se a deorum simulacrorum depraedatione abstinuisse laudatur?
pairs.question_en: Of what city was that Fabius the destroyer, who is praised for keeping himself from plundering the statues of the gods?
pairs.derivation: Anchored to Fabius via the detail that he abstained from plundering the gods' statues; single place answer (Tarentum), supported verbatim ('Tarentinae urbis euersor'). Closed-book: Fabius Maximus's recapture of Tarentum (209 BC) is historical.

pairs.source_text: Romulus et Remus asylum constituisse perhibentur, quo quisquis confugeret ab omni noxa liber esset, augere quaerentes creandae multitudinem ciuitatis.
pairs.question: Qui asylum Romae constituisse perhibentur, quo confugientes ab omni noxa liberi essent, ut multitudinem ciuitatis augerent?
pairs.question_en: Who are said to have established an asylum at Rome, so that those fleeing to it would be free from all harm, in order to increase the city's population?
pairs.derivation: Anchored by the deed (founding the Roman asylum to enlarge the population); two-name answer (Romulus et Remus), supported verbatim. Closed-book: the asylum of Romulus is a standard part of Rome's foundation legend. 'perhibentur' kept to match the text's hedged attribution.

pairs.source_text: qui tamen suis litteris credunt Arionem Methymnaeum, nobilissimum citharistam, cum esset deiectus e naui, exceptum delphini dorso et ad terras esse peruectum.
pairs.question: Quo animali Arion Methymnaeus, citharista nobilissimus, e naui deiectus ad terras peruectus esse fertur?
pairs.question_en: By what animal is Arion of Methymna, the renowned citharode, said to have been carried to land after being thrown from a ship?
pairs.derivation: Anchored to Arion of Methymna (named, 'nobilissimus citharista'); single answer (a dolphin, ablative Delphino), supported verbatim ('exceptum delphini dorso... ad terras esse peruectum'). Closed-book: the tale of Arion and the dolphin (Herodotus 1.23-24) is very famous. Augustine cites it as pagan lore ('suis litteris credunt'), hence 'fertur.'

pairs.source_text: Vnde Paulinus noster, Nolensis episcopus, ex opulentissimo diuite uoluntate pauperrimus et copiosissime sanctus, quando et ipsam Nolam barbari uastauerunt, cum ab eis teneretur, sic in corde suo, ut ab eo postea cognouimus, precabatur.
pairs.question: Cuius urbis episcopus erat Paulinus, quem Augustinus, cum de barbarorum uastatione ageret, commemorat?
pairs.question_en: Of what city was Paulinus, whom Augustine mentions in connection with the barbarian devastation, the bishop?
pairs.derivation: Anchored to Paulinus ('Paulinus noster'); single place answer (Nola, the see of which he was bishop), supported verbatim ('Nolensis episcopus'). Closed-book: St. Paulinus of Nola is a well-known figure; Augustine reports his prayer when Nola too was sacked by the barbarians.
